newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania Tarom airline restructuring gets new wings.
newsitem.headline: Romania Tarom airline restructuring gets new wings.

text.p: Romania's new government is relaunching a restructuring programme, headed by aircraft purchases, for state airline Tarom SA, but privatisation is not a priority for the moment, a top official said on Friday.
"We are behind schedule with Tarom's restructuring plan. We decided to speed it up, actually to relaunch it," Dan Popescu, Secretary of State at the Reform Ministry, said in an interview.
"Our strategic target now is to buy eight Boeing aircraft, the next generation 737, and to see what we can do for long-haul flights."
The airline, he said, was in the market for a replacement for its Airbus 310s, possibly with McDonnell Douglas MD-11s Combi.

Tarom's restructuring plan was initiated in 1995. But the project stalled under the leftists who had held power from the ousting of Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in 1989 until their defeat in last November's elections.
Popescu said Tarom has already done much to shed the image of uncomfortable aircraft and surly service inherited from the communist era.
But it now faces stiff competition on its domestic routes from private Dac Air operating slick Canadian-made DASH-8 aircraft and from a number of other airlines.

Tarom's international network, which includes most cities in western Europe plus U.S. flights, operates with a fleet of Soviet-made Tupolevs and Antonovs and Romanian-made British Aerospace Plc BAC 1-11s. It also has a number of newer Airbus and Boeing aircraft.
Transport Minister Traian Basescu said the new centrist cabinet was determined to back Tarom's plans to compete in the fast-growing Eastern European air market.
"We sent Boeing a letter saying the government will provide all financial guarantees for the deal," he said.
Popescu said the government had already approved a series of projects intended to improve its performance.
On Thursday, Tarom signed an accord with British Petroleum to create a $8.0 million joint venture to upgrade aircraft fuelling at Romania's main airports.
Last December, Tarom leased two French-made ATR aircraft for tests pending a decision on replacing ageing and noisy Soviet-vintage AN-24s on domestic flights.
Popescu said a privatisation plan, announced by Tarom three years ago, was not being examined for the moment.

"There is such a plan. But privatisation of Tarom will be considered later," he said in reference to a 1994 study by Western experts recommending Tarom be privatised through a combined public share offer and worker-management buyout.

Popescu said Tarom was still posting losses, but gave no details. The airline has laboured under huge debts in recent years and high tariffs paid to the Romatsa RA air traffic control authority added to its financial burden.
"Romatsa's tariffs drastically Tarom's costs. Something must be done to clarify this issue," Popescu said.
"However, things have improved a bit. Last year Tarom launched a programme to upgrade its logistics and consequently it managed to cut by 50 percent the losses recorded in 1996."
